claims.text: The selected alloy is a homogeneous, compositionally disordered, multi-element HEA with a bcc or similar crystal structure at room temperature.
The room-temperature alloy may contain local variations in chemical order despite appearing elementally homogeneous.
Cryogenic cooling reduces thermal atomic motion.
Reducing thermal motion by cooling below about 10 K promotes local atomic reordering into short-range chemically enriched clusters.
Nanoscale chemically ordered or enriched regions emerge within the disordered matrix during cryogenic cooling.
The proposed local clusters modify the electronic density of states.
The proposed clusters produce enhanced electron density and stronger electron–phonon interactions.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling caused by local clustering promotes Cooper-pair formation and induces superconductivity.
A compositionally homogeneous bcc Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 HEA is a conventional type-II superconductor with intermediate electron–phonon coupling and a critical temperature near 7.5 K.
Local structural disorder can influence superconducting properties in disordered superconducting materials.
The selected alloy is expected to enter a superconducting state at a critical temperature in the several-kelvin range.
Below its critical temperature, the selected alloy should exhibit a sharp resistivity drop and a magnetic-susceptibility anomaly characteristic of type-II superconductivity.
At room temperature and above the critical temperature, the alloy exhibits normal metallic rather than superconducting behavior.
The room-temperature starting state lacks enough local chemical order to enhance electron–phonon coupling.
The proposed local-reordering mechanism is limited to temperatures below approximately 10 K and compositions similar to known superconducting HEAs.
Changes in elemental ratios or processing that prevent local ordering may suppress the proposed superconducting mechanism.
